planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized grafted trees in late winter while still dormant, in deep, well-drained soil; Tejas tolerates the thin, alkaline soils and limited rainfall of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau better than most grafted pecans.

directions: Tejas is a long-standing Texas pecan selection associated with the USDA research station at Uvalde and valued for decades across drier parts of the state for handling thin, alkaline soils and restricted rainfall better than most grafted pecans. It carries useful field resistance to pecan scab, the fungal disease that forces heavy fungicide programs on susceptible cultivars in humid regions, making it a practical lower-spray choice for home orchards in drought-prone areas. Nuts are medium-sized and crack out reasonably well, though kernel fill and yield are more modest than newer high-production releases. As with other pecans, plant it alongside a genetically different cultivar for reliable cross-pollination and give it the generous mature spacing a full-sized pecan tree requires.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized grafted trees in late winter while dormant; Apache is an older selection from the USDA pecan breeding program at Brownwood, Texas, part of a series of releases given Native American tribal names.

directions: Apache is an older USDA pecan release from the Brownwood, Texas breeding program, part of the well-known series of cultivars given Native American tribal names alongside Cheyenne, Choctaw, and Comanche. It produces a well-filled, good-quality nut and was planted across parts of the southern Pecan Belt during the mid-to-late twentieth century, though newer scab-resistant releases from the same program have largely replaced it in new commercial plantings. Bearing specimens still turn up in older home orchards and variety trial blocks. Because it lacks the built-in scab resistance of later releases, it generally needs a regular fungicide program in humid climates and should be paired with a different pecan cultivar for cross-pollination.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized grafted trees in late winter while dormant; Shoshoni is an older USDA release grown historically for its large, attractive nuts across parts of the central and southern Pecan Belt.

directions: Shoshoni is an older USDA pecan release best known for producing large, attractive nuts on a vigorous tree, and it was once grown as both a shade and nut tree across parts of the central and southern Pecan Belt. It tends toward pronounced alternate bearing, swinging between a heavy crop one year and a light one the next, and like many pre-scab-resistance-era cultivars it needs attentive fungicide management in humid regions to protect foliage and nut fill. Today it is found mainly in older orchards and collector or variety-trial plantings rather than new commercial blocks, having been superseded by more disease-resistant modern releases. Plant it with a different pecan cultivar nearby to ensure reliable cross-pollination.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant, onto locally hardy seedling rootstock; Major is a wild-selected northern pecan long grown by cold-climate orchardists for ripening a crop within a shorter growing season than southern cultivars need.

directions: Major is one of the longest-grown named selections among cold-climate pecan enthusiasts, chosen from a wild native tree found well north of the commercial Pecan Belt for its ability to mature a crop within the shorter growing season of USDA zone 5 and 6 plantings. It is valued by Northern Nut Growers Association members and other cold-climate orchardists more for dependability than for nut size, since northern wild-type pecans run smaller and thinner-shelled than grafted southern cultivars. Graft it onto locally hardy seedling rootstock and plant it with a different cold-hardy pecan cultivar nearby, since pecans are wind-pollinated and need a genetically distinct pollenizer to set nuts well. Expect slower establishment and a longer wait to first bearing than is typical of pecans grown in the traditional southern Pecan Belt.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant, onto locally hardy seedling rootstock; Greenriver is a historic wild-tree selection kept in circulation by cold-climate pecan growers for its reliability at the northern edge of the species range.

directions: Greenriver is a historic wild-selection pecan kept in cultivation primarily by Northern Nut Growers Association-affiliated growers rather than by commercial southern pecan breeding programs, valued for dependable nut maturation at the northern margin of the pecan growing range. Like other northern selections, it trades nut size for hardiness, producing smaller, thinner-shelled nuts than the grafted cultivars bred for Gulf South production. Site it in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, and plant a genetically distinct pecan cultivar nearby since it cannot pollinate itself. As with other far-northern pecans, plan for a long juvenile period of many years before the tree begins to bear.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter while dormant, onto locally hardy seedling rootstock; Witte is one of the named wild-tree selections long maintained by northern pecan hobbyists for cold-climate reliability.

directions: Witte is another of the named wild-tree selections long grown by northern pecan hobbyists seeking cultivars able to mature a crop within the short growing seasons found well north of the main commercial Pecan Belt. It is maintained in Northern Nut Growers Association collections and university nut-planting trials as part of the small group of cold-hardy northern pecans distinct from the scab-resistant southern cultivars bred for Gulf South conditions. Its nuts run smaller and thinner-shelled than those of southern grafted cultivars, trading size for reliability in a cold climate. Plant it with a different pecan cultivar nearby for pollination and expect a long juvenile period before it begins bearing.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry
